title: HoneyMonkeys
subtitle: Microsoft goes looking for trouble
description: How Microsoft's Strider HoneyMonkey system finds malicious websites before they find you, what it uncovered in its first month, and what Microsoft is (and isn't) doing with what it learns.

beats.t: This is Security Now! Episode 2, August 25, 2005. We recorded this one over Google Talk, which came out yesterday. The ringtone alone is worth it.
Today's topic comes from Microsoft Research: the Strider HoneyMonkey Exploit Detection System.
Strider HoneyMonkey. Folks, try to guess what that is.
Start with honeypots. A honeypot is a closely watched computer left out on the Internet on purpose, so attackers will hit it and researchers can see what's out there.
Like Winnie the Pooh. Put out the honey and see who sticks their nose in.
Right. That's how security firms catch new worms. Microsoft flipped it around: instead of waiting to be attacked, its machines go out and visit dangerous websites.

beats.title: Honeypot vs. HoneyMonkey
beats.t: A honeypot waits to be attacked, which is good for catching worms that scan the network. A HoneyMonkey is a client honeypot: it browses to websites like a person would, to catch sites that attack visitors' browsers.
"Monkey see, monkey do." The HoneyMonkeys copy a person browsing with Internet Explorer, going to the kinds of sites that get people infected.
"Strider" is the name of a family of Microsoft Research projects. There's also Strider Gatekeeper, which detects spyware, and Strider GhostBuster, which detects rootkits.
Each HoneyMonkey is a virtual PC, a whole Windows machine in a file. If it gets infected, you just throw it away and start fresh.
The web has something like 10 billion pages, and most are harmless, so they start in the bad neighborhoods: block lists people post online, and links from spam and phishing emails.
The monkey doesn't click anything. It loads the page, waits a few minutes, and then the other Strider tools check whether anything on the machine changed.
So if the machine changed just from viewing a page, that page attacked it.

beats.title: Drive-by downloads
beats.t: A drive-by download is when a web page exploits a browser bug to install software just because you visited. You don't have to click or agree to anything. That's exactly what HoneyMonkeys are built to detect.
They test each suspect site in stages: unpatched XP, then XP SP1 with patches, then SP2 unpatched, then SP2 fully patched.
If a page still infects a fully patched SP2 machine, it's using a zero-day, a hole Microsoft hasn't fixed yet.
In the first month, the HoneyMonkeys found 752 URLs that tried to infect Internet Explorer using known vulnerabilities.
And they found one zero-day. Microsoft knew about the bug but had never disclosed it, and a website was already exploiting it.
Within two weeks, 40 more sites were using the same unpublished exploit.
So security through obscurity doesn't work. You don't have to tell anyone; the bad guys find out anyway.
The exploit sites are also connected. Among the top 30, many have the same owners, with registrations in more than ten countries.
One person owned the number 1, 3 and 10 sites, and 61 other exploit sites redirected visitors to him.
Infecting people's machines has become a business: spyware, adware, and zombie PCs for sending spam.
That's why it's gotten so much worse. It used to be kids showing off. Now there's money in it.

beats.title: Why the money matters
beats.t: Once infected PCs could be turned into cash through ad fraud, spam relays and stolen data, malware went from a hobby to an organized business. Attackers started sharing exploits and sending victims to each other's sites.
Most of the exploiting URLs were adult sites. No surprise to anyone who's been online a while.
Isn't that skewed by where they looked?
A little. The starting lists came from block lists people share. But they also found a shopping site and freeware download sites that attack visitors directly.
And more than 20 malicious search sites. Just running a search there tries to infect you.
So: stay out of the seedy parts of the web, stick with the big, well-known sites, and patch.
Some articles said this proves patching works. Who ever doubted that? Put an unpatched XP machine on the Internet without a firewall and it's game over.
Google, Yahoo! and MSN all had these bad URLs in their search results. Microsoft removed them from MSN Search.
And told Google and Yahoo!, I hope?
No. It also only tests Internet Explorer, not Firefox or Netscape.

On the positive side, results go to Microsoft's Internet Safety Enforcement Team, which works with the FBI to go after these sites. And there's a good reason not to publish the list: they're watching those sites for new exploits.
The catch is that the HoneyMonkeys come from a known block of IP addresses. Attackers will notice and block them, so Microsoft is talking about spreading them out around the world.
I'm glad they're being proactive, but using it for a competitive edge bothers me. The security tradition is to share.
Security is becoming a business for Microsoft, with anti-spyware and antivirus products coming. The good news is that they published how it works, so anyone can build their own HoneyMonkeys.
Other platforms have holes too. Apple just shipped 44 security fixes in one update. If Microsoft keeps working this hard, Windows could someday be the safer one.

quiz.q: How is a HoneyMonkey different from a traditional honeypot?
options: It visits websites to get attacked, instead of waiting to be attacked
quiz.explain: A honeypot waits for attacks. A HoneyMonkey goes looking for them by browsing suspicious sites like a person would.

quiz.q: How did a HoneyMonkey decide that a site had attacked it?
options: The site asked for a password
Its machine changed just from loading the page
quiz.explain: It only loaded the page and waited. If anything on the machine changed, the page had exploited the browser (a drive-by download).

quiz.q: How many exploit URLs did the HoneyMonkeys find in their first month?
quiz.explain: They found 752 URLs that tried to infect Internet Explorer, including one using a vulnerability Microsoft hadn't disclosed.

quiz.q: Why did Steve and Leo have mixed feelings about the project?
options: Microsoft only cleaned up its own search engine and only tested IE
quiz.explain: Microsoft removed the bad sites from MSN but didn't tell Google or Yahoo!, and it only tested Internet Explorer.

quiz.q: What did the zero-day discovery show?
options: Attackers can find and share bugs even when vendors don't disclose them
quiz.explain: One site exploited an undisclosed IE bug, and 40 more sites were using it within two weeks. Keeping it quiet didn't keep it secret.
